THE ZERO MACHINE PREPARED FOR COUNSEL
THE ZERO MACHINE
How Madwell Was Turned into a Financial Reservoir, Drained, and Left Behind
MADWELL EVIDENTIARY SYNTHESIS | COUNSEL BRIEFING DECK | SEPTEMBER 2, 2026
Abstract. This brieﬁng ﬁnds that Madwell, an indepen-
dent creative and marketing agency headquartered in Brook-
lyn, was converted from a real operating company into a ﬁnan-
cial reservoir. David Eisenman commissioned the reporting
result before Daniel Tucker entered Madwell. Tucker, ﬁrst de-
ployed through Anchin’s outsourced-accounting channel and
then installed as Madwell’s chief ﬁnancial ofﬁcer on November
1, 2018, professionalized and operated the resulting architec-
ture. Greg Wank was Anchin’s outsourced-accounting engage-
ment partner, Marc Newman coordinated the deployment and
was Tucker’s identiﬁed supervisor, and Michael Belfer was the
relationship and tax partner who later appears at basis and
exit-planning gates. The structure exploited the difference be-
tween cash and accrual bookkeeping so that value could be
suppressed, held, released, reassigned, and ultimately left be-
hind as debt and obligation.
Madwell was not a conventional fee-only advertising
agency . It operated more like a vertically integrated pro-
duction studio. The company conceived campaigns and
then, through Madwell and its controlled production network,
made much of what it had conceived: commercials, music,
live events, physical sets, experiential installations, and li-
censed merchandise and apparel. That distinction determined
the economics. If an agency bills a client $100, pays an un-
related production vendor $70 at cost, and keeps a $30 fee,
the $70 is a genuine pass-through. But when Madwell or a
Madwell-controlled production company performed the work,
the same $70 represented business conducted inside the enter-
prise: revenue, cost, margin, labor, and enterprise value. Call-
ing both situations “pass-through” erased the difference be-
tween money Madwell merely transmitted and work Madwell
actually sold and produced.
A subsequent contract-to-cash reconstruction closes that
economic-origin layer. In the same 2018–2023 period, an in-
dependent line-level remap recovers $123.750 million of V eri-
zon/Visible activity—89.70 percent of Madwell’s $137.966 mil-
lion of ﬁled gross receipts for all clients combined. The broader
2018–2024 V erizon-family ledger schedule totals $137.996 mil-
lion, only $30,009 above the entire six-year ﬁled topline. Mean-
while, native client and job ﬁelds carry $121.658 million of
BILL.com Paid objects to one controlled client or entity ad-
dress, including $84.842 million inside the 1072 clearing pop-
ulation. The visible ﬁled company was therefore almost one
client while the internal and payment records preserved a
much larger multi-client production economy . Those client ad-
dresses identify whose work generated the obligations; they do
not by themselves identify the ﬁnal recipient of pooled cash.
That false equivalence became the Zero Machine. Hay-
ley Rogers was Madwell’s ﬁrst in-house Vice President of
Finance—the ﬁrst person beyond outside accountants and out-
sourced ﬁrms to hold a senior ﬁnance position inside the com-
pany . Beginning in 2017, she built an internal system that at-
tached client, project, labor, card, bill, bank, and ledger iden-
tity to the same economic work. Eisenman selected the re-
quired accounting result in 2018. Through Madwell’s estab-
lished relationship with Belfer and Anchin, Tucker replaced
Rogers’s identity-preserving design with a ﬁnance-controlled
system of spreadsheets, imports, hosted books, clearing ac-
counts, deferred-revenue schedules, and paired journal entries.
Equal revenue and cost could be removed together; related-
company production could be treated like an at-cost outside
payment; revenue and direct cost could be deferred, reversed,
or moved between entities and periods; and the locally bal-
anced ledger would preserve gross proﬁt while making the
larger company disappear. In January 2022, for example, Mad-
well’s ordinary proﬁt-and-loss statement showed $5.712 mil-
lion of income, $2.643 million of direct cost, and $3.069 mil-
lion of gross proﬁt. Tucker’s leadership package presented the
$3.069 million gross-proﬁt remainder as “SALES.” The com-
pany did not become a $3.069 million business. Its $5.712 mil-
lion of activity had been compressed into its margin.
Across 2018 through 2023, Madwell’s six internal year-end
statements recorded $279.544 million of Total Income, while
its ﬁled partnership returns reported $137.966 million of gross
receipts. The difference—$141.578 million—is the amount of
internally recorded topline subjected to the zeroing treatment.
It was not an accounting convention applied only at year end.
The same method appears in paired eliminations of revenue
and cost of goods sold (COGS), monthly deferral and rever-
sal entries, related-company reductions, gross-proﬁt-as-sales
presentations, intercompany accounts brought back to zero,
and different ﬁnancial packages prepared for company lead-
ers, lenders, tax authorities, and government programs.
QuickBooks account 1072 was the machine’s principal cash-
release chamber. It was not a bank account. It was a synthetic
clearing account inside the books connected to BILL.com, Mad-
well’s bill-payment platform. A pooled withdrawal from Mad-
well’s bank could fund a bundle of BILL.com payments; the in-
dividual vendor objects were then posted against 1072 until the
clearing account returned to zero. The aggregate bank move-
ment and the individual payment stories balanced in Quick-
Books, but the clearing layer separated the cash leaving the
bank from the identity , payment proﬁle, and ﬁnal destination
of each purported vendor payment. Tucker wrote that 1072
“should usually be zero.” The point of the account was there-
fore not to preserve cash in place, but to permit cash to leave
through a pooled channel while the ledger erased the interme-
diate imbalance.
The second release rail was older. Bernard D. Malaky
was Eisenman’s former roommate and friend when Eisen-
man and co-founder Christopher Sojka—Madwell’s commer-
cial and creative leader—established Madwell in 2010. In 2011,
Malaky supplied a disclosed startup credit accommodation
and offered the founders practical use of the card and pay-
Conﬁdential work product - prepared for counsel 1

===== PDF PAGE 2 =====
THE ZERO MACHINE PREPARED FOR COUNSEL
ment setup. The accommodation was not necessarily fraudu-
lent when created, but it established the topology later used by
the Zero Machine: company activity could appear under Mad-
well or Eisenman on the issuer and accounting side while Mad-
well’s bank released the exact same amount under an outside
individual’s identity . From 2018 through 2024, the canonical
bank record contains 242 Bank of America automated-clearing-
house (ACH) withdrawals bearing Bernard D. Malaky’s name
and totaling $23.114 million. The same amounts reappear
as American Express (AMEX) payments and Madwell card-
liability entries across multiple card endings and book ac-
counts. In operational terms, that was the rail: once the ACH
left Bank of America under Malaky , the books treated the cor-
responding Madwell AMEX liability as settled and the cash
was outside Madwell. The old arrangement remained active af-
ter BILL.com became dominant and was used throughout 2022
and 2023, making it both the precursor to the later architecture
and a retained fallback within it.
Hong Kong provides a contained demonstration of the same
inversion. Sojka won the Danone/Nutricia client business
and Madwell built a Hong Kong operating afﬁliate to perform
it. Tucker’s August 2021 “Financials for David” package ﬁrst
showed a conventional proﬁt and loss with HK$19.811 mil-
lion of income, HK$14.296 million of cost of goods sold, and
HK$5.515 million of gross proﬁt. Later in the same package,
media billings and cost of goods sold were zero and the same
HK$5.515 million gross-proﬁt remainder occupied the Total In-
come position. Bank records separately show Madwell U.S.
sending $7.996 million to Madwell Hong Kong and receiving
$1.797 million back, while QuickBooks intercompany account
16030—the account meant to record what the U.S. and Hong
Kong companies owed each other—was returned to zero after
write-off and reversal entries. The ledger closed; Madwell U.S.
remained $6.199 million out of pocket.
The structure also changed what outside institutions were
asked to believe. It put more than $6.5 million of federal pan-
demic relief, forgiveness, and tax credits at issue: $2.148 mil-
lion of ﬁrst-round Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) pro-
ceeds, $1.938 million of second-round PPP forgiveness, and
a $2.51 million Employee Retention Credit (ERC) claim. The
ﬁrst PPP receipt was followed the same day by a $1.5 mil-
lion repayment to Madwell’s Bank of America revolving credit
line. For the second PPP round, 99.55 percent of the qualify-
ing revenue decline signed by Tucker as chief ﬁnancial ofﬁ-
cer came from the pass-through category , while fee revenue
declined only 0.79 percent. On the day Tucker signed the
second-round forgiveness recertiﬁcation, Madwell borrowed
$4 million, combined it with other company cash, wired $5
million to Eisenman for a balance screenshot, and received the
money back. ERC workpapers separately preserve a $1.628
million “Plan to delay” around the governing receipt thresh-
olds and a qualifying-wage population expanded across suc-
cessive Tucker workbooks. The zeroing system did not merely
describe the company after the fact; it supplied the revenue,
payroll, liquidity , and eligibility inputs presented to the gov-
ernment.
Bank of America ﬁnanced the reservoir while the same re-
porting structure obscured where the borrowed capacity went.
Madwell’s revolving credit line rose from $4 million to $6
million as reviewed statements and compliance certiﬁcates
went missing, covenant failures accumulated, and Madwell
liquidity entered related companies and personal or property
routes. In 2022, Madwell borrowed $2.6 million and sent it
to Eisenman’s personal account; $2.384 million is traced into
195 Throckmorton, a property-holding company allocated to
Eisenman, while Madwell retained the debt. By May 2023,
Bank of America demanded $4.75 million in repayment. The
ﬁnal amendment ended the revolving feature, imposed acceler-
ated repayment and liquidity restrictions, and pledged related
operating companies as guarantors. The beneﬁt had moved;
the debt, defaults, liens, guarantees, and operating burden re-
mained with Madwell.
The cash side supplies a second vantage point on the
same object. QuickBooks 1072 records $118.908 million of
disbursement-side movement. The broader direct-AMEX
bank family adds $23.889 million. Crediting $1.048 million
of identiﬁed inbound cash items produces $141.749 million
of net release through 2024. That cash ﬁeld is only $171,072
greater than the $141.578 million statement ﬁeld—a difference
of 0.12 percent. The near-closure does not mean that every sup-
pressed dollar has already been assigned to a ﬁnal beneﬁciary .
It means the operation has a measurable stock–ﬂow body: the
amount removed from Madwell’s visible economic scale and
the amount released through its two principal rails are two in-
dependently reconstructed views of virtually the same six-year
machine.
Transaction records show how the machine stole within
that ﬁeld. It changed vendor payment destinations and the
names, addresses, tax identities, and payment methods at-
tached to them; funded card payments whose reporting obli-
gation moved away from Madwell; marked obligations paid
or received without the represented cash settlement; returned
and reissued payments through clearing; preserved duplicate
payment states; routed company borrowing to personal, prop-
erty , and afﬁliate endpoints while Madwell retained the debt;
converted a failed company wire into false Sojka owner his-
tory; stripped client and project identity during the migration
from the original QuickBooks Desktop ledger to QuickBooks
Online and Ramp, the successor accounting and payment plat-
forms; and continued rewriting bills, vendors, payment meth-
ods, credits, and tax records after Madwell stopped operat-
ing. The chronology begins with the 2011 Malaky precursor,
turns on the 2017–2018 displacement of Rogers and installa-
tion of Tucker, follows Tucker’s recurring production layer—
Russell Ieong inside Madwell and M&S Global, the outsourced
accounting ﬁrm formally known as Manubhai & Shah LLP—
and ends with the 2024 drain, the incomplete transfer of con-
trol, Madwell’s April 2025 closure, and continued post-close
reconstruction. The $141.578 million reservoir is the measured
ﬁeld in which the paper identiﬁes the speciﬁc thefts, private
and afﬁliate beneﬁts, false settlements, government and lender
consequences, burden shifts, and remaining endpoint popula-
tions. The company created the value. The Zero Machine re-
moved its identity , released the cash, and left Madwell carry-
ing what remained.
Keywords. ﬁnancial fraud; misappropriation; cash–accrual
arbitrage; clearing accounts; identity substitution; false settle-
ment; stock–ﬂow reconstruction; payment systems.

THE ZERO MACHINE PREPARED FOR COUNSEL
1 T echnical Summary
Finding. Madwell’s ﬁnancial records do not describe an ac-
counting anomaly . They describe a theft system. Real client
work and company borrowing supplied value; accounting
treatments removed the activity from the company’s visible
scale; two controlled cash families released it; identity , settle-
ment, and lifecycle changes obscured its destination or reas-
signed its burden; and the 2024 transfer left the depleted com-
pany with Sojka. The system is visible at statement, rail, trans-
action, and control levels at once.
Controlling operation-level ﬁnding. The Zero Machine was
a theft operation. “Exﬁltrated” is the governing verb for the
Madwell value captured in the $141,578,371.18 ﬁeld and released
through the controlled cash architecture. No afﬁrmative innocent
population has been established inside that ﬁeld. Endpoint un-
certainty grades the proof and last visible destination of partic-
ular portions; it does not reopen whether the operation existed.
Future work allocates the operation among techniques and end-
points. It does not relitigate it.
The paper calls the mechanism the Zero Machine . It
performed four linked jobs. It fed on the value created
by a real operating company . It zeroed that value by re-
moving equal revenue and cost, separating client iden-
tity from ledger identity , and preserving gross proﬁt
while shrinking reported scale. It drained company
cash through QuickBooks 1072/BILL clearing and the
Malaky-named AMEX rail. It then reassigned debts, pay-
ment histories, owner activity , vendor identities, and
post-transfer obligations so the visible company and its
remaining owner carried the terminal condition.
The system has a measurable shape. Internally
recorded activity exceeded ﬁled gross receipts by
$141,578,371.18 from 2018 through 2023. Movement
through the two cash-release families, after the net cash-
item offset, totaled $141,749,443.50 through 2024. The
difference is $171,072.32, or 0.12 percent. Those mea-
surements are two views of the same reservoir, not two
amounts to add. The $141.578 million ﬁgure measures
the value subjected to the zeroing system; transaction re-
construction identiﬁes the speciﬁc theft routes, beneﬁts,
burden shifts, and last visible endpoints inside it.

Redirected payouts, false settlement, duplicate or recycled releases, per-
sonal/property and afﬁliate deployment, owner-history inversion, and
post-close cleanup.
The operator succession is chronological. A disclosed
2011 credit accommodation created the ﬁrst identity-
separated topology . In 2017–2018, Hayley Rogers, Mad-
well’s ﬁrst in-house Vice President of Finance, held
responsibility while decisive authority remained with
Eisenman and the outside professional channel. Eisen-
man selected the required reporting result; Tucker con-
verted it into a repeatable control system; M&S Global,
the outsourced accounting ﬁrm formally known as
Manubhai & Shah LLP , and the inside ﬁnance layer
produced it; and the successor QuickBooks Online
and Ramp systems carried the record through trans-
fer, collapse, and post-closure reconstruction. The open
institution-held records concern the ﬁnal ownership of
particular lots and the legal measurement of loss. They
do not erase the theft architecture already visible in the
company , bank, ledger, and platform records.

THE ZERO MACHINE PREPARED FOR COUNSEL
2 Introduction
This paper’s conclusion is direct: Madwell’s ﬁnance appara-
tus became a system for stealing value from the company , dis-
guising the release, and transferring the remaining burdens to
the company and owner left behind. The system depended
on Madwell being real and successful. Christopher Sojka,
Madwell’s co-founder and commercial and creative princi-
pal, led the clients, ideas, pitches, production, and commer-
cial work that created the value. David Eisenman, Madwell’s
co-founder and chief executive, controlled banking, account-
ing, tax, and the outside-ﬁnance channel through which that
value could be redeﬁned and moved. The fraud begins in the
distance between those two realities.
The accounting problem grew out of a real industry
convention. An advertising agency may collect $100
from a client, pay an unrelated vendor $70 at cost, and
keep a $30 fee. The $70 is a genuine pass-through
and can properly be presented net. Madwell’s model
was different when Madwell or an afﬁliated production
company performed the work and earned margin on
it. In that setting, applying the same pass-through la-
bel removed activity that belonged to the business itself.
Equal revenue and cost could disappear together, gross
proﬁt could remain, and the statement would still bal-
ance. A $100 engagement could therefore appear as $30
of sales without a visible arithmetic error.
The ﬁrst relevant structure predates the six-year recon-
struction. In 2011, Bernard Malaky offered a disclosed
credit accommodation so the young company could ﬁ-
nance equipment. Madwell used the credit while the up-
stream identity remained Malaky’s. The arrangement is
not proved fraudulent at its inception. It nevertheless
created an early separation between company use, pay-
ment authority , card identity , and company-facing ac-
counting. Eisenman operated at the point where those
surfaces met. The same identity split remained available
years later, after a more elaborate payment and account-
ing system had been installed.
The control problem became visible in 2017 and 2018.
Hayley Rogers, Madwell’s ﬁrst in-house Vice President
of Finance, was responsible for payroll, vendors, report-
ing, close, and the integration of client, project, card,
bank, and ledger records. She did not control the de-
cisive bank, wire, card, hiring, or outside-accounting
gates. The October 2017 books described a proﬁtable
company with positive working capital and $6.845 mil-
lion of receivables plus unbilled revenue, yet Rogers
and her husband supplied household funds to protect
payroll. On December 29, a large receipt from Happy
Family , a major baby-food client, an American Ex-
press payment, payroll, Eisenman, and Michael Belfer—
the Anchin partner who managed Madwell’s outside-
accounting relationship—converged in the same cash
crisis. Eisenman returned from the professional channel
saying, “we have a plan.”
In 2018, Eisenman speciﬁed the reporting result be-
fore Daniel Tucker held Madwell’s ﬁnance function.
Four months of labor journals totaling $3.043 million
on each side were moved out of the operating months
so client views retained hard costs but not employee
labor. When the entries were restored and produced
an approximately $714,000 ﬁrst-quarter loss, Eisenman
called the result wrong without identifying a transac-
tion error. During Rogers’s maternity leave, he pri-
vately opened Madwell’s books to Anchin’s outsourced-
accounting general manager. Tucker then inherited
Rogers’s process and access. By November, he was Mad-
well’s chief ﬁnancial ofﬁcer and had placed the company
inside Bank of America’s CashPro portal, BILL.com’s
payment system, QuickBooks, ﬁnance-controlled work-
papers, and the Swizznet remote-hosting environment
that he and Eisenman controlled at the decisive gates.
The scale is visible from two directions. Madwell’s six
internal year-end income statements report $279.544 mil-
lion of Total Income for 2018 through 2023. Its ﬁled part-
nership returns report $137.966 million of gross receipts
for the same years. The $141.578 million difference is
the amount this report describes as designated for ze-
roing. A separate reconstruction of movement through
QuickBooks account 1072 and BILL.com clearing, the
Bernard D. Malaky/American Express rail, and the net
unclassiﬁed-check offset totals $141.749 million through
2024. The difference between the two views is $171,072,
or 0.12 percent. The ﬁgures are not additive damages
and do not assign each incoming dollar to a particular
recipient. They show the same six-year ﬁnancial ﬁeld
from the accrual and cash sides.
The cash side has two recurring families. Quick-
Books account 1072 and BILL.com provide the princi-
pal clearing path. Bank of America separately records
242 debits totaling $23.114 million under Bernard D.
Malaky . The same amounts appear as American Express
payments and as card-liability entries in QuickBooks.
Their timing and aggregate behavior track the clearing
ﬁeld across the full period, including the 2024 terminal
movement. The record therefore supports treating the
Malaky/American Express population as the second rail
rather than accepting the card-liability label as the end of
the inquiry . American Express’s master-account hierar-
chy , native settlement identiﬁers, funding proﬁles, cred-
its, rewards, and refund destinations remain the records
that identify the rail’s ﬁnal endpoint.
The same control logic appears at transaction scale. A
January 2022 proﬁt-and-loss statement reported $5.712
million of income, $2.643 million of direct cost, and
$3.069 million of gross proﬁt; the leadership package
called the gross-proﬁt remainder “SALES.” Madwell
borrowed $2.6 million and sent it to Eisenman’s personal
account; after partial returns and a later company addi-
tion, $2.384 million reached his 195 Throckmorton prop-
erty entity while Madwell retained the debt. In 2024, a

company-to-company wire that failed by $45 and was
then successfully resent became $2.200 million of gross
Sojka owner activity in QuickBooks. These examples
concern different forms of value, but each depends on
the same ability to change what an amount meant as it
crossed a boundary .
The ﬁnal phase occurred while ownership and ﬁnan-
cial control were separating. Belfer’s tax work mod-
eled Eisenman’s exit. Sojka was still ﬁghting for bank,
card, and ledger access as the sale was being structured.
On October 3, 2024, Sojka paid Eisenman $1.325 mil-
lion under an agreement requiring complete control to
be delivered. Eisenman retained 195 Throckmorton, the
property-holding company funded through the traced
debt route, and Discofries, a related cannabis company .
Sojka received Madwell with debt, defaults, near-empty
liquidity , and incomplete permissions. After Madwell
stopped operating in April 2025, the Tucker Associates
BILL console remained attached for ﬁve more months,
and named QuickBooks Online and Ramp user accounts
continued changing records.
The report now proceeds in strict order. A short pre-
cursor chapter explains the early identity structure and
the 2017–2018 transfer of ﬁnancial control. The quarter
sequence then follows what entered the modeled ﬁeld,
what left through the two rails, which dated transactions
or actions mattered, and what condition carried into the
next quarter. The appendices preserve the larger proof
sets, attribution limits, source routes, and institution-
held records needed to close ﬁnal recipients and conse-
quences.
2.1 The visible company was essentially one client
The later contract-to-cash reconstruction supplies the
economic baseline the stock–ﬂow body requires. Mad-
well ﬁled $137,966,104.00 of gross receipts for all clients
combined from 2018 through 2023. An independent,
same-period line-level remap recovers $123,749,782.98
of V erizon/Visible activity , or 89.6958 percent of the en-
tire ﬁled company . The older 2018–2024 V erizon-family
schedule records $72,141,098.00 of recognized revenue
and $65,855,015.00 of pass-through—$137,996,113.00 in
total, only $30,009.00 above Madwell’s entire ﬁled 2018–
2023 topline. Because the periods differ by one year, that
second comparison is a scale control rather than an iden-
tity equation. The same-period remap is the governing
test.
The internal side is nearly twice as large. Adjusted
client inﬂows total $279,551,475.94, while the six inter-
nal statements record $279,544,475.18 of Total Income.
The $7,000.76 difference is immaterial at this scale. The
picture is therefore not a small agency that happened to
handle some pass-through cash. It is a large multi-client
operating company whose ﬁled topline was compressed
until almost the entire visible company resolved to V eri-
zon/Visible alone.
The contract corpus gives that scale economic mean-
ing. Client agreements distinguish fees from outside
costs, require approvals, preserve audit rights, and gov-
ern non-markup, rebate, credit, and vendor-payment
treatment. Those rules establish whose money entered
Madwell and what the company was permitted to do
with it. They also explain why a client or project address
surviving in the payment system is probative: it ties an
obligation to the work that generated it even when the
pooled cash rail later loses the recipient chain.

3 Methods, Data, and Evidentiary
Standard
3.1 The question is how the system stole, not
whether the ledgers balanced
The reconstruction treats the ﬁnancial operation as one
system observed from several sides. The ﬁrst measure-
ment identiﬁes the value absorbed into the zeroing ﬁeld.
The second measures cash released through the recur-
ring rails. The third follows individual episodes through
obligation, authorization, payout, identity change, set-
tlement, return or retention, book and tax treatment, and
the last independently visible holder. A platform la-
bel such as Paid, a clearing-account row, or an aggre-
gate card settlement is therefore a waypoint, not the eco-
nomic event.
The paper states people, institutions, and systems in
full before relying on shorthand. In the technical sched-
ules, QuickBooks Online is abbreviated QBO; Quick-
Books Desktop and QuickBooks Enterprise are QBD and
QBE; accounts payable and accounts receivable are A/P
and A/R; proﬁt and loss is P&L; general ledger is GL;
remote deposit capture is RDC; know-your-customer
ownership records are KYC records; BILL.com Funds
Transfer Detail is FTD; Bank of America is sometimes
BofA; and the U.S. Small Business Administration is
SBA. Form 1065 is Madwell’s federal partnership return,
Schedule K-1 reports each owner’s share, and Form 1099
is the information return used here for vendor-payment
reporting. GF 620 Park and 195 Throckmorton were
property companies allocated to Sojka and Eisenman,
respectively . CSDE, Goldﬁnch, and Discofries were re-
lated cannabis businesses; Starﬁsh, Millwright, and Tiny
Giant Sounds were related production or operating com-
panies. An IOLTA account is a lawyer’s trust account
used here as the last visible settlement door.
3.2 Evidence hierarchy
First-party bank, ledger, platform, workpaper, ﬁling,
contract, and communication records control. Repro-
ducible validation packages control derived counts.
Later falsiﬁcation and canonical reconstructions super-
sede earlier hypotheses. Integrated narrative products
organize chronology but do not overrule native records.
Automated ﬁlename, timestamp, duplicate, and version
inferences are routing aids only .
3.3 Stock–ﬂow identity
For quarter q, the modeled carried difference is
Sq = Sq−1 + Dq − Rq,
where Dq is the quarter’s modeled statement-ﬁeld input
and Rq is measured or allocated cash-side release. For
2018–2023, annual input equals internal Total Income
less ﬁled gross receipts. Internal annual totals are dis-
tributed across quarters by observed quarterly general-
ledger income; ﬁled receipts are distributed by recon-
structed customer-receipt timing. QuickBooks 1072
movements and the 242 canonical Malaky-named ACH
withdrawals are transaction-dated. The 87 other AMEX-
coded cash exits are allocated using the observed Malaky
timing distribution. The net unclassiﬁed-check offset is
allocated using receipt timing. The opening boundary is
S2017 = 0.

The cash-side control is
R = 118,907,831.50 QuickBooks Online 1072 credits
+ 23,889,198.00 AMEX-coded cash exits
− 1,047,586.00 net unclassiﬁed-check offset
= 141,749,443.50.
The American Express component contains 242 Malaky-
named automated-clearing-house withdrawals totaling
$23,113,582.79 and 87 other American Express-coded
cash exits totaling $775,615.21. Within the Malaky pop-
ulation, issuer statements or controlled workpapers re-
cover 202 events totaling $20,560,504.46; 40 events to-
taling $2,553,078.33 remain without event-level issuer

T able 2. Evidence classiﬁcations used throughout the reconstruction
Record-closed A bank debit, check image, platform event, journal, message, contract, workpaper, ﬁling, or exact
reconciliation establishes the stated ﬁeld.
Integrated ﬁnding Multiple independent source families establish a functional pattern or causal sequence even though
no one record states the whole conclusion.
Modeled quantity A stated allocation rule converts annual observations to quarters or reconciles independent projec-
tions. The rule and sensitivity are disclosed.
Endpoint production The local archive stops at an issuer, processor, bank, tax authority , lender, or platform. The paper
names the exact next record instead of treating an intermediate state as the ﬁnal door.

rows. QuickBooks Online American Express-liability
entries close the bank total through $23,113,577.35 of
ordinary components plus one $5.44 bank-only event.
These are addresses on the same population, not addi-
tive amounts.
The company books call the Malaky-named ACH pop-
ulation card-liability settlement. The paper does not
accept that label as the endpoint. The held records
show company cash leaving under Bernard D. Malaky ,
the same amounts reappearing as AMEX payments and
Madwell liabilities, a persistent identity wall across mul-
tiple card endings and book accounts, and behavior
that closes the same macro ﬁeld as 1072/BILL. Those
facts establish AMEX/Malaky as the second release
rail. Native AMEX hierarchy , funding, settlement,
merchant/acquirer, credit, reward, refund, and proﬁle
records will separate ordinary expense settlement from
replaced payment, credit absorption, return, or other
endpoint use inside the rail; they are not a prerequisite
to recognizing the rail itself.
3.5 Sensitivity and nonadditivity
Uniform within-year allocation preserves every annual
year-end state and the terminal $171,072.32 overage, but
changes the intra-year path. The maximum quarter-end
deviation from the governing allocation is $6,652,655.73
at 2019 Q3. Accordingly , the paper treats annual accu-
mulation, drawdown, and terminal closure as robust;
exact quarter shape is model-dependent. The quarter
ﬁgures are a disciplined temporal model, not observed
quarter-end cash balances.
The statement ﬁeld, cash ﬁeld, BILL object surface,
AMEX event surface, false-settlement face value, muta-
tion populations, and direct-beneﬁt examples overlap.
They are never added as damages. Returns, voids, reis-
sues, and book versions are linked lifecycle states. A
second release is counted only when a second inde-
pendently settled, non-returned value transfer is estab-
lished.
The 2024 ﬁgures show no new ﬁeld input because no 2024
internal-versus-ﬁled comparator is in the model. “N/A” is the ev-
identiary statement. A computational zero is used only to model
discharge of the $15.116 million state carried from 2023. The
$171,072.32 terminal overage is not a negative bank balance or
a newly identiﬁed beneﬁciary .

5 The Precursor and the Hinge,
2011–2018
5.1 A legitimate accommodation created the
prototype
In 2011 Bernard Malaky openly offered personal credit
so the young company could ﬁnance equipment. He
allowed Sojka and Eisenman practical control of the
card and payment setup. By 2013 Madwell was pay-
ing liabilities carrying Malaky or Bernard identity across
AMEX, Citi, and Barclays while Eisenman explained the
arrangement to the company’s accountant. The accom-
modation was not proved fraudulent at inception. Its
importance is structural: company use, upstream iden-
tity , payment authority , and company-facing account-
ing could occupy different surfaces while Eisenman op-
erated the point where they met.
5.2 Rogers inherited responsibility without the
decisive gates
By 2017 Madwell was proﬁtable and growing quickly .
October records showed $16.347 million of revenue,
$7.555 million of gross proﬁt, $957,298 of net income,
$6.845 million of receivables plus unbilled revenue, and
positive working capital. The liquidity crisis was real,
but it was not an operating-loss story . Long client terms,
accelerating media spend, early AMEX paydowns, and
incomplete planning compressed cash inside a prof-
itable company .
Rogers built QuickBooks Online classes and locations,
project proﬁt-and-loss statements, gross client revenue
and pass-through separation, card substantiation, receiv-
able discipline, and Harvest labor journals. Yet she was
not on the Bank of America account, could not wire,
lacked full card credentials, and repeatedly encountered
side plans. She and her husband supplied $225,000 and
then another $85,000 to keep payroll moving. On De-
cember 29, as an American Express payment, payroll, a
receipt from the major baby-food client Happy Family ,
Eisenman, and Belfer collided, Eisenman returned from
the professional channel saying, “we have a plan.”
5.3 The result came before the replacement operator
In May 2018 Eisenman directed a hard-cost-only client
view and moved four months of labor journals totaling
$3,043,033.25 on both sides to December 31. When the
entries were restored and produced an approximately
Conﬁdential work product - prepared for counsel 10

===== PDF PAGE 11 =====
THE ZERO MACHINE PREPARED FOR COUNSEL
$714,000 ﬁrst-quarter loss, he called the result wrong
without identifying a transaction error. During Rogers’s
maternity leave he privately gave Anchin’s outsourced-
accounting general manager access, acknowledged that
QuickBooks Online might notify her, and asked how to
tell her.
The replacement proceeded before the explanation.
Tucker mapped Rogers’s process, replaced her on V er-
izon ﬁnance, inherited access, and reversed the labor-
accounting position after initially appearing to support
it. After she left, Tucker held the QuickBooks Online
password, became the functional and then formal chief
ﬁnancial ofﬁcer, installed Madwell inside the superior
BILL.com console belonging to Tucker Associates, con-
centrated administration of Bank of America’s Cash-
Pro portal with Eisenman, and consolidated the master
ledger, workpapers, connectors, backups, and recovery
state in the Swizznet hosted environment. The reporting
preference had become infrastructure.
6 State-Space Reconstruction
The state does not remain full sized. Its longitudinal sec-
tion expands when the quarter’s designation exceeds rail
release and contracts when release exceeds designation.
The gold, red, and navy traces are independent ﬂux mea-
surements; the teal body is the cumulative state that rec-
onciles them.
The tube is a state-space visualization, not a bank account or a claim
that particular dollars remained physically segregated. Its cross-
sectional area encodes the modeled carried ﬁeld. The outer traces
encode quarter entry and rail release on separate common scales.
The diagonal is equilibrium: quarters below it added
to the carried state; quarters above it drew the state
down. Marker area adds the third dimension. The trajec-
tory shows that the machine did not operate at one ﬁxed
size or one ﬁxed rate.

7.3 Mechanism Plate: The Malaky / AMEX
Dual-Identity Rail
The visual does not treat the card-liability label as proof of an ordi-
nary payoff. It shows the reason the population behaves as a rail:
cash leaves the bank under one persistent upstream identity while
the issuer and books preserve the same amount under different
company-facing identities. The ﬁnal endpoint remains an AMEX
production question.

11.6 Mechanism Plate: T wo Owner Roundtrips, T wo
Record Treatments
Both circuits return to company cash; neither is a permanent cash-
loss amount. The evidentiary difference is the record treatment: the
Sojka circuit was visible and reversed, while the Eisenman circuit
was absent from the supplied controlled QBO population. That dif-
ference matters to how ownership history and liquidity were later
presented.

12.5 Mechanism Plate: The Written Zeroing
Controller
The controller can force the book state to zero without proving cash
settlement. The feedback loop is the bank test. It divides the exact
population into supported and bank-disproved routes; the $6.835
million face amount is an accounting-state population, not a sepa-
rate cash-theft total.

13.4 Mechanism Plate: Failed-Wire Hysteresis
Hysteresis means the output state depends on the path taken, not
merely the original input. The bank event was a company-to-
company transfer that failed, returned $45 short, and then suc-
ceeded. The later edit path converted that event into gross owner
activity more than twice the transfer amount.

14 Real bills supplied the camouﬂage
The payment system did not separate ordinary vendors from an adverse rail. It used the same vendors through different routes,
often inside the same year, quarter, month, or day . That is the operational point: a recognizable vendor and a real obligation could
supply the commercial story while the system selected a different cash route, payment state, or invoice allocation for the individual
transaction.

What the evidence establishes. The complete BILL population
contains 10,499 Paid objects totaling $188.010 million. Within
it, 7,368 objects totaling $120.048 million were assigned to 1072
and 3,131 totaling $67.963 million were assigned elsewhere.
The $188.010 million is a platform denominator, not another
loss amount.
Why real bills do not answer the operation. A real obligation ex-
plains why a payment-shaped record existed. It does not prove
which Madwell funds satisﬁed it, whether the same bank event was
assigned to another obligation, whether the vendor proﬁle changed,
or where the release ultimately settled. The legitimate business sup-
plied the camouﬂage.

22 Conclusion: one operation, carried through to exit
The evidence is not a collection of anomalies. It is one chronological operation. Madwell created value in public. Eisenman selected
the result. Tucker professionalized the method and controlled the decisive systems with Eisenman. The method removed the com-
pany’s scale while preserving the chosen remainder; the payment architecture released a nearly identical ﬁeld; the historical books
were rebuilt during the exit; and the depleted company and its obligations were transferred to Sojka while superior control persisted.

Controlling conclusion. Madwell’s controlled ﬁnancial system removed $141,578,371.18 from the company’s reported economic iden-
tity , released a nearly identical amount through the principal payment architecture, rewrote the historical source record during the exit,
and transferred the depleted company and its obligations to Sojka. The two macro amounts are overlapping views of the same operation,
not additive damages. Real bills do not create an innocent partition; they supplied the substrate through which route, state, identity ,
and obligation could be changed.
What remains open is allocation, not existence. American Express, BILL, Intuit, banks, the IRS, and Anchin hold the records needed to
identify terminal recipients, physical operators, payout proﬁles, tax adjustments, and precise consequences within the ﬁeld. Those records
can complete attribution. They do not reopen whether the operated system existed.

B AMEX/Malaky Competing-Hypothesis T est
B.1 Chronology
The earliest documented topology is a disclosed 2011 credit accommodation, not a proved fraud at inception. By
2013, historical bank records preserve Bernard/Malaky descriptors across American Express, Citi, and Barclays. In
2016–2017, 57 Bank of America-funded American Express-liability rows totaling $6,263,203.10 carry Malaky/Bernard
descriptors. The later BILL.com/CashPro/Swizznet stack scales a topology in which upstream identity , company-
facing use, accounting treatment, and payment authority can remain on different surfaces.
After BILL.com became dominant, the old rail remained live. In 2022 it carried 29 settlements totaling $2,017,425.87
across ten months; in 2023 it carried 16 totaling $315,622.13 across eleven months. All 45 close by exact date and cents

B.2 Population and hypotheses
The broad American Express-coded cash family contains 329 events totaling $23,889,198.00. The canonical Malaky
subset contains 242 Bank of America events totaling $23,113,582.79; the other 87 events total $775,615.21. Within the
canonical subset, 202 events totaling $20,560,504.46 close to issuer statements or controlled workpapers; 40 totaling
$2,553,078.33 do not. The full bank amount closes to QuickBooks Online American Express-liability treatment through
$23,113,577.35 of ordinary components and one $5.44 bank-only event.
The ordinary-settlement and release-rail hypotheses are not rhetorical positions; they make different document
predictions. Ordinary settlement predicts a native issuer settlement ID binding the company-bank debit to the cor-
porate card hierarchy and its charge obligations. Release-rail use predicts a different funding proﬁle, parent account,
credit/refund path, or duplicate external payment of the represented expense. The held record is sufﬁcient to identify
the cash exit and identity wall, but not to inspect the decisive native issuer ﬁelds. Cap-and-penny limits, a second
hidden-card ﬁle, INDN-as-recipient, zero visible matches, and a complete self-cleaning refund loop are withdrawn
theories and are not used.
C QuickBooks 1072 and BILL Endpoint Geometry
The canonical 1072 surface contains 7,368 BILL.com Paid objects totaling $120,047,590.39. It is an object-level view,
not the same grain as the $118,907,831.50 QuickBooks Online credit-side macro control. The last-local-door partition
is exact:
• 3,877 objects / $63,119,253.90: exact native bank batch/member;
• 1,895 / $37,484,673.86: bank clearing without a native individual member;
• 1,534 / $17,012,858.66: BILL object only;
• 55 / $2,140,677.87: individual named bank payee; and
• 7 / $290,126.10: partial native batch.
The named-payee class ﬁxes the cash-side payee, not receiving-account ownership or entitlement. The remaining
classes end at a platform, aggregate batch, or incomplete bank surface. Payment-time vendor/proﬁle history , pay-
out token, processor disbursement, generated or negotiated check, receiving-account ownership records, and vendor
acknowledgment are the last-door production.
The difference between the 7,368-object surface and the QuickBooks Online credit-side macro view is $1,139,758.89.
It is a representation-perimeter difference, not a beneﬁciary or loss. The paper keeps those grains separate.
D Worked Evidence Chains
D.1 A client job crosses from workpaper to bank rail
A sealed 2020 bridge joins 29 workpaper job codes to BILL by complete job-code preﬁx, then to payment objects by
controlled vendor/invoice key , and ﬁnally through Funds Transfer Detail and native bank batches. Seventeen codes
recover 87 invoice objects totaling $2,314,151.39, or 80.8923 percent of the $2,860,779.40 workpaper actual-cost popu-
lation. Eighty-four obligations totaling $1,093,456.91 travel through 1072; three totaling $1,220,694.48 travel directly
through account 10010. This is an executable job-to-obligation-to-rail bridge; it does not assert that workpaper rev-
enue, cost, accrual, invoice, and bank movement are additive.
D.2 Zarbee’s: receipt, suppression journal, and funded vendor children

ber/date label but a different native transaction ID, $171,009.03 of account-1072/Bank of America funding. That
funding closes to a native bank event, BILL.com batch, and nine children. The same journal context and client/job

D.3 The two $25,000 exits on August 19, 2024
Two authenticated cash exits occurred on the same date and for the same amount. Chase account 7672 sent a $25,000
wire to Fatking Films and QuickBooks Online reduced the accounts-payable balance. Separately , Bank of America
sent $25,000 under the Malaky/American Express descriptor, closing to issuer card 1003 and an American Express-
liability journal. An older date-and-amount join fused their attributes. The current record preserves both objects and
uses the collision as a negative control: exact date and cents alone do not establish identity .
E Accounting Mechanics and False Settlement
Madwell’s integrated model makes gross-versus-net presentation the primary statement mechanism. Where Mad-
well or an afﬁliate performed work and earned margin, equal revenue and cost could be removed while gross proﬁt
survived. Six internal statements total $279,544,475.18 of Total Income; six ﬁled returns total $137,966,104.00 of gross
receipts; the difference is $141,578,371.18.
The written false-settlement procedure creates a different result. Equal accounts payable (A/P) and accounts receiv-
able (A/R) can be marked Paid and Received through method Other, equal-and-opposite bank-ledger entries can net
to zero, and reconciliation can close without the represented cash movement. Of 108 exact pairs totaling $10,562,497.34,
65 totaling $3,727,761.77 are bank-supported and 43 totaling $6,834,735.57 are bank-disproved. The 65 are mandatory
controls; the 43 prove false represented settlement, not an equal amount of stolen cash.
F Control Planes, Migration, and Post-Closure Reconstruction
Bank of America’s CashPro portal divided maker and approver roles while concentrating root administration. In the
bounded native audit, all 368 successful Payment IDs were ﬁnally approved by Tucker or Eisenman; 359 complete
maker/approver lifecycles used different creating and approving accounts. BILL.com remained under the Tucker
Associates console from Oct. 31, 2018 until Oct. 3, 2025. The Swizznet hosted environment held the master ledger,
workpapers, connectors, backups, and recovery state.
The migration from QuickBooks Desktop to QuickBooks Online preserved all 1,587 numeric 2022–2023 fee-revenue
rows totaling $49,673,519.50; it did not delete the revenue dollars. It did strip Client/Project identity from all 232
matched account-40065 journal rows while preserving date, number, memo, and amount. Ramp then inherited an
incomplete object and vendor lineage. Its lifetime denominator is 913 bill objects totaling $14,734,087.01; platform
states such as Paid manually, Ready for payment , and Ready for release are not external settlement.
Named QuickBooks Online and Ramp accounts for Bautista, Wright, Paul, Gupta, and Varma continued exact-
object work after operations ceased. The record closes account-level coordination across 149 shared QuickBooks On-
line objects, including four touched by all three principal named QuickBooks Online accounts, plus 113 QuickBooks
Online-to-Ramp handoffs. Authentication and session records remain necessary for physical-user attribution.
G Corrections and Negative Controls
The following controls are part of the ﬁnding, not footnotes against it:
• Ten ordinary one-bank-event-to-many-BILL allocations totaling $1,014,217.28 show that pooled allocation can be
legitimate.
• A $150,000 SiriusXM bank payment is genuine; four later BILL objects reconstruct its allocation. It is not a false-
payment or nonreceipt row.
• Sixty-ﬁve intercompany pairs totaling $3,727,761.77 have bank support and remain beside the 43 disproved pairs.
• HITENY’s $43,000 was funded by a sibling entity; “unfunded Paid” is withdrawn.
• Paciﬁc World to Proyecto is a native vendor merge, not an unresolved identity fork.

• Positive BILL Funding Return values are usually actual bank debits; one Creative Peaks $23,500 event is the closed

H Actor and Attribution Ledger
The body table controls the concise actor chronology . Four attribution rules govern the appendices. First, system
capability is not proof that every object was altered. Second, a named platform account is not automatically the
natural person at the keyboard. Third, custody of Tucker-derived records proves provenance and continuity , not
collusion. Fourth, functional hierarchy can be established from recurring control at gates without inventing a literal
employment or supervision relationship not in the record.
I Beneﬁts, Burdens, and Nonadditivity
The reconstructed beneﬁts and burdens are stated by episode. Direct routes include the 195 Throckmorton prop-
erty transaction, related-entity liquidity deployment, owner-history inversion, temporary roundtrips, and selected
corporate-card or processor paths. Burdens include company debt, vendor obligations, employee and contractor
shortfalls, lender and tax presentation, and post-transfer liabilities. A beneﬁt amount is not automatically loss; re-
turned funds are not permanent loss; gross deployment is not net retention; and institution reliance or assessed gov-
ernment loss requires the institution’s own records.
No amount in the paper is added merely because it appears in more than one layer. The statement spread and
cash release are paired projections. BILL and 1072 are container/object representations. AMEX charges and settle-
ments overlap. False-settlement face value measures represented obligations. Mutation and post-close counts are
investigative surfaces. The same economic episode is counted once at its terminal result.
J Institution-Held Completion Records
1. American Express: master account and card hierarchy; native settlement and funding identiﬁers; authorized users;
merchant/acquirer settlement; credits, rewards, refunds, and cash redemption; know-your-customer ownership
records.
2. BILL: historical vendor and proﬁle versions; payment-time vendor ID, network ID, and payout token; Sent-
Pay/processor disbursement; VCard settlement; generated, negotiated, voided, and reissued checks.
3. Ramp and Divvy: native payment ID and account; processor settlement; source-object lineage; card creden-
tial/device history; credits and refunds.
4. Banks: receiving-account identiﬁers, automated-clearing-house and wire addenda, negotiated check images and
endorsements, know-your-customer ownership records, onward movement, and property/title records.
5. Intuit and hosted systems: authentication, session, IP/device, audit, migration, deletion, merge, and export his-
tory sufﬁcient to attribute physical users and recover prior states.
6. T ax, lender, and government institutions: submitted packages, signers, corrections, decisions, reliance, forgive-
ness/refund treatment, examinations, assessments, and calculated loss.
7. V endors and clients: acknowledgments, remittances, invoice and payment histories, contractual rebate/credit
treatment, and unpaid-obligation records.

K Proof Grades, Limitations, and Validation
The proof ladder is P0 capability/control; P1 mutation or state conﬂict; P2 cash to an intermediate platform; P3 named
counterparty or bank payee; P4 receiving-account owner conﬁrmed; P5 retention or onward use conﬁrmed; P6 ad-
verse diversion and resulting beneﬁt or burden proved. P0–P2 are not labeled theft. P3 does not establish beneﬁcial
ownership. P4 and P5 still require entitlement and purpose analysis.
The central limitations are explicit. The quarterly path depends on within-year allocation even though annual
results do not. The source archive does not yet enumerate every $141.578 million statement-ﬁeld dollar as a lot. Bank
cash is fungible, so job, journal, batch, and amount conservation establish controlled bridges but not title to dollars
absent unique identiﬁers. Some platform exports omit historical proﬁles, payout tokens, or settlement records. Legal
conclusions, intent, damages, government loss, and physical-user identity are outside the mechanical ﬁndings unless
the cited record closes them.
The release validator checks quarter coverage, all current denominators, source-route closure, removal of super-
seded language, appendix continuity , PDF searchability , absence of absolute local paths in the rendered document,
and the package hashes. Mechanical validation does not substitute for source interpretation.

N Contract and Economic-Substance Register
The contract records establish the commercial rules surrounding fees, budgets, outside costs, approvals, audit,
markup, rebates, credits, and vendor payment. Components from the same instrument are nested and are not added
to the instrument total.

Q Canonical Operation Finding and Non-Regression Rules
The operation-level ﬁnding controls future synthesis. The Zero Machine produced exﬁltrated Madwell value; sup-
pressed topline fed it; the zeroing regime processed that value; QuickBooks 1072/BILL.com clearing and Bernard D.
Malaky AMEX were its principal release rails; the identiﬁed principal and operator hierarchy controlled it; and the
depleted legal company was transferred to Sojka as the exit mechanism.
The $141.578 million ﬁeld is not reduced to a neutral presentation difference. Missing endpoint records do not
create an innocent remainder. Real vendor payments do not prove that the suppressed ﬁeld funded those payments.
Malaky AMEX is not reduced to an ordinary card-settlement label. The ownership transfer is not described as a rescue
after an unrelated collapse. Future work grades techniques, last visible destinations, and concealed endpoints inside
the established operation.
